The report further recommends that the City adopt an asset management framework, including assigning roles and responsibilities for pedestrian facilities management, adopting a uniform asset condition rating system, and establishing a mechanism for ongoing data maintenance. The major pilot findings are summarized below and key implementation actions are reflected in the recommendations of this report. Subsequent to the completion of the pilot report, but prior to the date of this report, the City Council approved a funding transfer to pay for the first year of the next phase of the citywide program (CF 21-1469-S4). documents.title: Report from Department of Transportation
documents.excerpt: CITY OF LOS ANGELES INTER-DEPARTMENTAL MEMORANDUM Date:​ ​ April 20, 2026 To:​ ​ Honorable City Council c/o City Clerk, Room 395 Attention: Honorable Heather Hutt, Chair, Transportation Committee From:​ ​ Laura Rubio-Cornejo, General Manager ​ ​ Department of Transportation Subject:​ PUBLIC RIGHT-OF-WAY INFRASTRUCTURE STATE OF GOOD REPAIR SUMMARY As directed by Council File (CF) 25-1142, this report outlines the public right of way assets managed by the Los Angeles Department of Transportation (LADOT), identifies industry standards for their maintenance and repair, and provides the necessary staff and funding required to bring all LADOT assets into a state of good repair. RECOMMENDATION That the Los Angeles City Council NOTE and FILE this report. BACKGROUND In December 2025, Council directed LADOT, as well as other relevant departments, to identify industry standards and best practices for the repair, replacement, and maintenance of public right-of-way infrastructure, and to determine the necessary staffing levels, equipment costs and materials, and fleet capacity needed to reach these standards. The California Vehicle Code (CVC) and Manual of Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD) grant local jurisdictions the authority to install traffic control devices. The Los Angeles Municipal Code (LAMC) section 80.07 gives LADOT the exclusive authority to install, place, maintain, or remove any traffic control device in the City of Los Angeles. LADOT may delegate its authority to another city agency to install or remove temporary no parking signs. This report provides an overview of the public right of way traffic control assets installed and maintained by LADOT, their lifecycle and current state of repair, and recommendations to bring each asset into a state of good repair. DISCUSSION As authorized by the CVC, MUTCD, and LAMC, LADOT manages all traffic control assets from curb to curb, including: The Honorable City Council​ 2​ April 20, 2026 ●​ Traffic signals ●​ Roadway striping and markings ●​ Traffic and parking signage ●​ Curb markings ●​ Traffic calming devices ●​ Bicycle facilities The industry standard, and best practice for these assets, is to proactively maintain a state of good repair through a preventative maintenance program. LADOT has previously managed a preventative maintenance program to ensure an ongoing state of good repair, but at current staffing levels maintains these assets through request based systems. As a result, many of the assets are currently in fair or poor condition. These assets are managed across several bureaus within LADOT, including District Operations, Field Services, ATSAC & Metro Programs, Parking Management, Project Development, and Capital Projects. Accordingly, the construction, repair, and maintenance of these assets is managed by a wide range of classifications including transportation engineers and aides, transportation planners, paint and sign posters, electricians, parking meter technicians, and others. documents.excerpt: FORM GEN. 160 (Rev. 8-12) CITY OF LOS ANGELES INTER-DEPARTMENTAL CORRESPONDENCE DATE: November 5, 2026 TO: The Honorable City Council FROM: Keith Mozee Executive Director and General Manager Bureau of Street Services SUBJECT: RESOURCES NEEDED TO MEET INDUSTRY STANDARDS OR BEST PRACTICES FOR PUBLIC RIGHT-OF-WAY INFRASTRUCTURE MAINTENANCE (CF 25-1142) RECOMMENDATION That the City Council note and file this report, as it is provided for informational purposes only. SUMMARY Pursuant to the recommendations adopted by the City Council on December 3, 2025 (Council File 25-1142), this report provides information pertaining to the resources needed to maintain and repair the City’s public right-of-way infrastructure, up to industry standards or best practices set by the City. For purposes of this report, the public right-of-way infrastructure types under the purview of the Bureau of Street Services (StreetsLA) are pavement preservation, pothole repair, alleyways, street sweeping, sidewalks, curb ramps, and street trees. Bringing these maintenance programs up to industry standards/best practices requires significant investment, in both on-going costs, as well as capital costs. DISCUSSION Pavement Preservation Program (Asphalt Roadways) StreetsLA manages a street network of approximately 23,000 lane miles (approximately 21,900 lane miles of asphalt streets, 1,100 lane miles of concrete streets, and 1,280 lane miles of alleys) through its Pavement Preservation Program (PPP), aiming to keep the City’s streets in a state of good repair. The United States Department of Transportation (USDOT) Federal Highway Administration (FHWA) provides policy, leadership, and research to assist State Departments of Transportation (DOTs) and local agencies in implementing effective pavement preservation. In 2020, FHWA published strategic elements to support the FHWA Pavement Preservation Program, with goals to preserve the nation’s roadway infrastructure in good condition using cost-effective pavement preservation. Primary industry technical standards are set by the American Association The Honorable City Council November 5, 2026 Page 2 of 10 of State Highway and Transportation Officials (AASHTO) for the design and rehabilitation of pavement structures. Individual streets within the City’s street network are surveyed and rated once every three years based on a Pavement Condition Index (PCI). In line with industry practice and standards, StreetsLA’s Pavement Preservation Program (PPP) includes pavement preservation treatments and corrective maintenance for the City’s 23,000 lane miles of streets. motion: I THEREFORE MOVE that the Council INSTRUCT the Bureau of Street Services, Bureau of Street Lighting, Bureau of Sanitation, Bureau of Engineering, Bureau of Contract Administration, and the Department of Transportation, with the assistance of the City Administrative Officer and any other relevant department, to report back in 60 days on the following: Identify industry standards or where more effective, other standards and best practices, for the repair, replacement, and maintenance levels/cycles and timely inspection of the public right-of-way infrastructure including but not limited to bike lanes, curb cuts, sidewalks, street trees, storm drains, street trees, and streetlights; Establish standards and best practices to guide the City’s funding and resource allocation; • Determine staffing levels, equipment costs and materials, fleet capacity needed to reach these standards; • Outline any additional costs or resources required to achieve best practices as defined by the Bureaus or Department; • Develop a phased approach, in one year increments, to meet best practices established by the City in five years, and identify resources and annual budget allocations necessary for each phase; and • Provide recommendations for ongoing updates or reassessments, such as options for applying formula based increases on a year-over-year basis. I FURTHER MOVE that the Council INSTRUCT the Department of General Services to report back within 60 days of the submission of the above outlined reports with information on fleet maintenance, repair, and storage needs of the proposed phases by the Bureaus and Departments. The report should include the amount of real estate available for fleet storage, real estate needed to accommodate the proposal, and the staffing and equipment needed to maintain the fleet and yards.
